slides.title: An alert raises two different questions
slides.line: Does a 90% catch rate mean a 90% issue chance after an alert?
points: Distinguish the system's catch rate from the chance an alerted order has an issue.
Keep your prediction; we will use base rates to check it.
slides.notes: Ask for a show of hands. Do not reveal the posterior yet; use the next slides to define outcomes and denominators.

slides.title: Predict which outcomes remain after an alert
slides.line: Which of the four order states include an alert?
points: List the complete cases first.
Do not assume the four cases are equally likely.
slides.notes: Give learners one minute to identify both alerted cases. Advance to the visual before discussing their shares.

slides.title: A probability starts with a defined outcome
Possible cases need not be equally likely
points: Count favorable outcomes only when the possible outcomes are equally likely.
Four named order states do not imply four equal probabilities.

slides.title: Try the fair-die shortcut on a new event
points: The favorable outcomes are 4, 5 and 6.
This count works because every fair-die face has the same chance.

slides.title: Predict what OR does with overlap
slides.line: Should a shared outcome be counted once or twice?
points: Write the two event sets.
Circle outcomes that belong to both.
slides.notes: Have learners mark the overlap before showing the visual. Ask why simple addition can exceed the union.

slides.title: AND keeps the overlap; OR counts it once
Event shares must satisfy probability bounds
points: Subtract the overlap once when combining events.
A proposed overlap cannot exceed either event.

slides.title: A complement can shorten the calculation
points: The event and its complement partition the sample space.
Check that the two probabilities add to 1.

slides.title: Predict the number of complete meals
slides.line: Two bases, three proteins, three sauces: add or multiply?
points: Imagine choosing one option at each stage.
Count complete routes, not individual ingredients.
slides.notes: Ask learners to sketch one full route and predict the total before revealing the stage diagram.

slides.title: A sequence has one choice at each stage
Count complete routes, then remove forbidden ones
points: Multiply the choices along a complete route.
Restrictions change the number of branches; count each valid route.

slides.title: A restriction changes the branches you multiply
points: The two fillings are distinct, so only five remain for the second slot.
This counts ordered fillings; ignoring order answers another question.

slides.title: Predict whether order changes the outcome
slides.line: Is assigning three roles the same as choosing a three-person team?
points: Imagine swapping two selected people.
Decide whether the result is a new outcome.
slides.notes: Have learners vote before advancing. A role assignment changes on a swap; a team does not.

slides.title: Order changes arrangements, not selections
The question determines whether order matters
points: Roles make order matter. A team does not.
Divide by the reorderings of each selected team.

slides.title: Two roles and two teammates have different counts
points: Swapping roles makes a new assignment.
Swapping names inside an unordered pair does not make a new team.

slides.title: Predict the denominator after given
slides.line: For on time given express, divide 15 by 80, 40 or 35?
points: Locate the express group first.
Keep the 15 express and on-time orders as the numerator.
slides.notes: Ask learners to choose a denominator without calculating. Reveal the order table on the next slide.

slides.title: Conditioning changes the denominator to the named group
The same numerator can answer three different questions
points: The same 15 orders answer three different questions.
“Given” selects the denominator before you divide.

slides.title: Transfer the denominator rule to late express orders
points: The express group has 40 orders, 25 of them late.
The direction of conditioning determines which group is counted.

slides.title: Independence means new information does not change the chance
Check independence with conditional and joint shares
slides.line: P(A | B) = P(A) when B gives no new information
points: The joint check is P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
Disjoint nonempty events cannot be independent.

slides.title: Predict which paths produce an alert
slides.line: Can an alert come from both an issue and an ordinary order?
points: Name the two disjoint routes.
Multiply along each route before adding.
slides.notes: Ask learners to identify both alert routes. Do not show the total until the weighted-path slide.

slides.title: Weight each path before adding its contribution
Total probability adds the weighted paths
points: Multiply within each issue-status path.
Add the two disjoint alert paths: 585 alerts per 10,000 expected orders.

slides.title: Use the complement to count no-alert orders
points: Alert and no alert cover every order in this model.
That is 9,415 no-alert orders per 10,000 expected orders.

slides.title: Predict the issue share among alerts
slides.line: Will the posterior be closer to 90% or 15%?
points: Compare the issue-alert and ordinary-alert paths.
Use all alerts in the denominator.
slides.notes: Ask learners for a prediction before showing the Bayes tree. Do not reveal the calculated posterior in Notes.

slides.title: Bayes reverses the question using base rates
An alert changes the chance, not the decision
points: The alert catches 90% of real issues; that is a different conditional chance.
Among alerted orders, most are ordinary because ordinary orders are far more common.

slides.title: Reverse the question for a negative alert
points: The denominator includes every no-alert order.
A negative alert lowers the issue chance without making it zero.

slides.title: Odds compare an event with its alternative
Convert probability to odds before updating
points: Turn probability into odds before applying the evidence multiplier.
Convert the updated odds back to probability.

slides.title: Predict what a second signal requires
slides.line: Can the same evidence multiplier be used twice automatically?
points: Ask whether signals are independent within each issue-status group.
Dependence changes the second signal's likelihood ratio.
slides.notes: Invite an explanation of what could make two signals related. The next slide makes the assumption explicit.

slides.title: Repeated evidence multiplies odds, not probabilities
A second signal needs a dependence assumption
points: A second signal multiplies odds only under the stated conditional-independence assumption.
Without that assumption, use the second signal’s conditional rates after the first.

slides.title: A negative second signal can reverse the update
points: The negative likelihood ratio is 1/3 under the same conditional-independence assumption.
Evidence can move a probability down as well as up.

slides.title: An alert decision needs probability and consequences
Report the posterior, assumptions and missing costs
slides.line: 15.4% issue chance among alerts ≠ a business decision
points: Report the model, base rate and uncertainty.
Compare review cost, missed-issue cost and available capacity before acting.

slides.title: Close with the question before the percentage
points: State which population and event the probability describes.
Then explain what additional costs or consequences the business decision needs.

slides.title: Predict the independent sample size
slides.line: Twelve orders, each timed twice: 12 or 24 independent units?
points: Name the unit that received a process assignment.
Repeated readings of one unit can be related.
slides.notes: Ask learners to vote before revealing the order plot. Count assigned orders, not stopwatch readings.

slides.title: Keep each order with its process
The observation unit determines what can be compared
points: Keep each time attached to its process.
Repeated readings of one order do not create new independent orders.

slides.title: The baseline depends on the question
The grand mean weights all observed orders
points: ANOVA weights each observed order.
An equal-weight average of group means answers a different question when group sizes differ.

slides.title: Predict where noise enters the comparison
slides.line: Could the same group means give weaker evidence?
points: Hold the group means fixed.
Imagine a wider spread of orders within each process.
slides.notes: Ask for a prediction before drawing the variation split. The noisy alternative appears later.

slides.title: Each order has a group gap and a within-group gap
The squared gaps split total variation
points: Total squared variation splits into between-group and within-group sums.
The within-group part is the noise estimate for the comparison.

slides.title: Mean squares divide variation by degrees of freedom
points: Three group means leave 2 between-group degrees of freedom.
Twelve orders minus three fitted group means leave 9 within-group degrees of freedom.

slides.title: The same group gap can have different noise
F compares between-group signal with within-group noise
points: The ratio compares mean separation with within-group noise.
More noise can make the same mean gaps less persuasive.

slides.title: Four times the within-group noise cuts F fourfold
points: The group means stay fixed while within-group SS rises from 24 to 96.
The evidence weakens even though the observed mean gaps do not move.

slides.title: The reference curve puts F in context
A right-tail area measures evidence under the null
points: Use the right tail of the F reference under equal population means.
The 5% cutoff is 4.2565; it is not the observed p-value.

slides.title: The noisy alternative sits near the 5% threshold
points: The right-tail area is much larger than for F = 18.5.
A 5% rejection still says nothing by itself about useful minutes saved.

slides.title: A global signal does not name the winning group
State the global conclusion within its scope
points: There is evidence that the population means are not all equal.
The global test does not identify every pairwise difference or a causal winner.

slides.title: Plan comparisons as one family
points: Plan the three comparisons as one family.
Bonferroni intervals control the chance of any missed interval at 5% under the model.

slides.title: Predict how many cells the design needs
slides.line: Two offers × two day types: how many combinations?
points: Draw every offer–day pairing.
Ask what replication each pairing needs.
slides.notes: Have learners sketch the four cells before showing the grid. Keep the separate retailer dataset distinct from the packing case.

slides.title: A two-factor design observes every combination
Replication belongs within each factor combination
points: All four combinations must be observed.
Independent replication within each cell supplies the error estimate.

slides.title: Cell means can differ from marginal means
Read combinations before averaging across them
points: A weekday bundle gain is $4; a weekend gain is $12.
The equal-day average gain of $8 does not describe either day by itself.

slides.title: A future day mix changes the average gain
points: The equal-day $8 gain assumes a 50–50 day mix.
This is a spending estimate for a hypothetical mix, not profit or a new observation.

slides.title: Main effects may miss a combination effect
Build a cell mean from grand, main and interaction effects
points: Main effects describe averages over the other factor.
Interaction adjusts the cell mean when the additive prediction misses.

slides.title: Predict whether interaction lines must cross
slides.line: If the offer gain changes by day, must the lines cross?
points: Compare their slopes rather than their endpoints alone.
Predict what nonparallel lines would mean.
slides.notes: Ask for a sketch of two nonparallel lines that do not cross in the plotted range. Reveal the chart next.

slides.title: Interaction changes an effect across contexts
A marginal average can hide a useful interaction
points: Nonparallel lines show changing sample effects; they need not cross.
A marginal average can conceal a valuable context-specific effect.

slides.title: Keep interaction separate from random error
Four variation sources add to the total
points: Separate offer, day, interaction and within-cell error variation.
With 8 residual degrees of freedom, MSE = 32/8 = 4 dollars².

slides.title: An interaction contrast measures the changing gain
points: The difference of differences isolates the changing bundle gain.
Its standard error is about $2.31; the matching interaction F is 12.

slides.title: One ANOVA table answers three different questions
Name each null before reading its F test
slides.line: F offer = 48  ·  F day = 75  ·  F interaction = 12
points: Each row tests a different null hypothesis.
Interpret interaction before promising one universal offer effect.

slides.title: Repeated readings need not be independent replications
Count independent units before trusting the table
slides.line: 12 independent transactions − 4 cell means = 8 error df
points: Counting duplicate records as independent inflates information.
Check assignment, residuals and similar error spread before trusting the table.

slides.title: One observation per cell leaves no error estimate
slides.line: 4 observations − 4 fitted cell means = 0 error df
points: A complete 2 × 2 grid alone is not independent replication.
Without residual degrees of freedom, this simple design cannot estimate within-cell error.

slides.title: A recommendation can depend on the combination
Compare uncertainty with the decision threshold
points: Recommend conditionally, with uncertainty and the intended sales mix.
Spending is not profit; margins, costs and study design still matter.

slides.title: Audit software output against the study design
slides.line: Check the model pieces before the software tail area
points: One-way: SSG = 98⅔, SSW = 24, F = 18.5.
Two-way: error df = 8, MSE = 4, interaction F = 12.
